Early 1990s. Fort Bragg flat range.

A 1st SFOD-D (Delta Force) operator running high-speed, live-fire pistol drills around steel barrels.

The loadout is pure perfection:

Silkies

White sneakers

Black ball cap & dark shades

Thigh-rig drop-leg holster

Custom combat pistol

An absolute unit of a 90s tactical mustache

Long before the internet era of $1,000 designer combat pants, high-cut carbon helmets, and tactical Instagram influencers, Tier-1 marksmanship was built on one thing: relentless, blistering repetition.

Delta assaulters spent countless hours burning through tens of thousands of rounds of ammunition on the flat range until drawing, driving the gun, and putting double-taps on target at point-blank speed became pure, subconscious instinct.

No plate carrier. No tactical fashion. Just peak physical conditioning, speed, and pure lethality.

Modern gear is great, but fundamentals never go out of style.

Drop a 🇺🇸 below to honor the golden era of Delta Force. Peak performance in the flesh.

America’s stealth destroyers are getting hypersonic missiles.

All three Zumwalt-class destroyers are being converted to carry Conventional Prompt Strike missiles.

These are hypersonic weapons — traveling at Mach 5 or faster — designed for rapid, long-range conventional strikes.

Each ship will carry 12 of them.

The Navy is removing the original large guns that never fully delivered and replacing that space with vertical launch tubes for these new missiles.

The Zumwalts were once criticized as expensive ships searching for a mission.
Now they’re being turned into the first surface ships in the U.S. fleet armed with operational hypersonic strike capability.

Supporters say this finally gives the class a clear, high-end role in peer competition.
Critics still question the cost, the limited numbers, and whether three ships with 12 missiles each will move the needle enough.

Game changer… or expensive niche capability?

Would you support a Sharia ban in your state’s courts?

Alabama and Tennessee have passed laws barring judges from applying foreign or religious law including Sharia when it conflicts with constitutional rights.

Supporters say the laws put the U.S. legal system first. Critics, including the Brennan Center for Justice, argue they target Muslims, while some legal scholars say they address a problem that doesn’t exist.

Should your state adopt a similar ban, or keep the law as it is?

NYC Mayor proposes $500 a month to families housing former inmates.

As part of his 88-page plan to close Rikers Island, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is expanding a program that pays families to house relatives returning from jail or prison.

The Kinship Reentry Housing Program currently supports about 50 families.
The new plan would grow that to 300.

Right now, participating households receive $500 a month for up to 12 months to help cover the cost of taking someone in.

The goal is to give people leaving incarceration a stable place to land instead of cycling back into the system or ending up on the street.

Supporters say family housing can reduce recidivism and ease pressure on the city’s jail population as Rikers is phased out.
Critics argue it’s another use of taxpayer money that rewards the wrong incentives.

Either way, it’s one of the more concrete pieces of the larger Rikers closure strategy.

Charlie Kirk said you cannot be a Christian and vote Democrat.

Resurfaced remarks from 2024 are circulating again.

Charlie Kirk argued that a true born-again Christian cannot vote for the Democratic Party, pointing to positions on abortion and gender ideology as fundamentally incompatible with biblical teaching.

He went further, saying that if you vote Democrat as a Christian, “you can no longer call yourself a Christian. You have to call yourself something else.”

The comments have sparked strong reactions on both sides.

Some see it as a clear moral line.
Others see it as political gatekeeping that oversimplifies both faith and politics.

Either way, the statement keeps forcing the same uncomfortable question into the open:
Where does personal faith end and party loyalty begin?

A widely shared clip of Marco Rubio comparing long-time American retirees to recent arrivals is sparking fresh debate online. In the remarks, Rubio argued that someone who worked 40 years can receive "$800, $900, a thousand a month" in Social Security while a recent arrival from Cuba can qualify for "$1,500 a month," adding that "it makes no sense" (InvestmentWatchBlog).

Official data adds important context to both sides of the comparison. According to the Social Security Administration and The Motley Fool, the average retired-worker Social Security check reached $2,092.17 a month as of October 2026, though lower lifetime earners or early claimers can receive much less. Meanwhile, qualifying Cuban and Haitian entrants do not receive Social Security retirement checks—they can access time-limited Office of Refugee Resettlement programs (such as Refugee Cash Assistance, capped at four months for eligibility dates on or after May 5, 2025) and means-tested aid if they meet income or family criteria (Administration for Children and Families).

Eleven states, Washington, D.C., and dozens of local bans could be on the line next week. On December 2, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court hears oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins the first time the justices are squarely weighing whether bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles violate the Second Amendment (SCOTUSblog, ANJRPC).

Gun-rights plaintiffs including the Second Amendment Foundationjoined by the U.S. Solicitor General—argue that tens of millions of Americans lawfully own AR-15-platform rifles, making them protected arms in common use (ANJRPC). Defending jurisdictions and gun-safety groups like Everytown argue the bans fit America's historical tradition of firearm regulation and give communities tools to reduce mass-shooting fatalities.

With a ruling expected by late June 2027, how do you think the Supreme Court should decide? Drop your take below.

Necessary protection for high-risk calls, or total overkill for local police? 🚁🌙

A photo of the Harris County Sheriff's Office SWAT (High Risk Operations Unit) in Texas is sparking debate online after operators were spotted running gear normally seen in Tier 1 military special operations units including quad-tube night vision, suppressed rifles, Multicam kit, a tactical K9, and air support.

Some argue specialized units facing armed barricaded suspects and cartel threats need every edge they can get, while others question whether non-military law enforcement should be outfitted like special forces.

Where do you stand smart investment in officer safety, or way too much military-grade gear for local policing? Drop your take below 👇

Rest in peace, Officer Jared Israel. 🕊️💙

The Cobb County Police Department is mourning the loss of Officer Jared Israel, who passed away on November 17, 2026. He joined the department on April 9, 2007, and dedicated more than 19 years of service to the Cobb County community.

Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, and fellow officers during this difficult time. Thank you for your service, Officer Israel.

This 747 is America’s flying doomsday command post.

There are only four of them in the entire fleet.

The E-4B Nightwatch looks like a regular Boeing 747 on the outside.
On the inside, it’s built to keep the U.S. government functioning even if the worst happens.

It’s hardened against nuclear electromagnetic pulse.
It can stay airborne for days with aerial refueling.
It carries secure communications so the President and top military leaders can still issue orders if ground command centers are destroyed.

Most people have never seen one.
Fewer realize these aircraft exist specifically for the unthinkable scenario.

It’s not a passenger jet.
It’s a flying war room designed to survive the end of the world as we know it.

Did you know it existed?

Did Nvidia's board make the right call bringing Jensen Huang back, or did this move catch you off guard? Drop your take below 👇

Before and after satellite imagery from Benghazi, Libya, today—Nov. 22, 2026. 🛰️💥

A suspected Ukrainian sea drone strike hit the Russian Navy corvette Mercury (Merkury) early Sunday morning while it was docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya.

Libyan officials said the vessel had stopped to refuel and resupply when it was struck, triggering an explosion and fire that heavily damaged the ship's stern and midsection. Commissioned in 2023 and officially part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, the Project 20380 warship is assessed by naval analysts as likely destroyed or severely crippled—while neither Moscow nor Kyiv has officially commented.

Look closely at the before and after comparison—how far can unmanned sea drones reach next? Drop your thoughts below 👇

#Ukraine #Russia #Benghazi

“CH-53K REFUELS IN MID-AIR WHILE SLING-LOADING AN F-35C STEALTH JET OFF THE COAST OF NEW JERSEY.”

In one of the most remarkable aviation feats in modern military history, a U.S. Marine Corps CH-53K King Stallion heavy-lift helicopter conducted an in-flight aerial refueling from a KC-130 Hercules while externally slinging a 22,000-pound F-35C Lightning II airframe over the Atlantic Ocean.

Piloted by Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron One (VMX-1) in coordination with the F-35 Integrated Test Force, the mission transported the carrier-variant stealth jet airframe from NAS Patuxent River, Maryland, to Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, New Jersey:

Unmatched Heavy-Lift Power: Powered by three General Electric T408 turboshaft engines producing 22,500 total horsepower, the CH-53K can carry an external payload of up to 36,000 pounds—nearly triple the lift capability of its predecessor in hot-and-high conditions.

Mid-Air Refueling Under Load: Connecting to the KC-130's refueling drogue with a 22,000-pound fighter suspended by steel cables required precision flight control, fly-by-wire stability, and steady rotor aerodynamics over open water.

Expeditionary Recovery (TRAP): The demonstration validated that the Marine Corps can execute long-range Tactical Recovery of Aircraft and Personnel (TRAP) for fifth-generation fighters across contested island chains and remote expeditionary advanced bases.

Infinite Operational Range: Combining heavy external sling capabilities with aerial refueling allows the King Stallion to transport heavy artillery, armored combat vehicles, and damaged aircraft across vast maritime distances without stopping.

American aerospace engineering operating at the absolute limit.

Rest in peace, Sgt. Sarah Beckstrom. 🇺🇸🕊️

D.C. National Guard soldiers, West Virginia National Guard members, and U.S. Marshals Service partners gathered in Washington, D.C. for emotional wreath-laying ceremonies honoring 20-year-old Sgt. Sarah Beckstrom, who gave her life protecting fellow troops while serving on Joint Task Force-District of Columbia.

As leaders reflected on her sacrifice, the D.C. National Guard noted that the wreaths were "a reminder that behind every uniform is a person, a family, a story and a future," adding that though she was only 20 years old, "her courage, dedication and willingness to serve left a legacy far greater than her years."

President Trump is putting a surprising spin on the latest breach at the FBI.

Speaking on Saturday after reports confirmed hackers breached the bureau's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database, Trump suggested the cyberattack could carry a "silver lining" — potentially exposing internal files related to Russia, Ukraine, and election fraud.

"I always like to put things in a positive spin," Trump said, while declining to share specific details about the intrusion itself.

The NCIC system serves as a nationwide lifeline connecting federal, state, local, and tribal police with fugitive warrants, missing-person alerts, and criminal records — making this the second major cyber incident to hit FBI systems since September.

Serious national security breach or a moment of unintended transparency? Drop your take below.

#FBI #Cybersecurity #Trump

Breaking news out of Louisiana tonight—an Amtrak passenger train has derailed after slamming into an 18-wheeler hauling a bulldozer. 🚨🚆

According to local police and Acadian Ambulance Service, Amtrak's Sunset Limited collided with the tractor-trailer around 6 p.m. along U.S. Route 90 near Thru-Way Park Road in Lafayette, close to Broussard, sending the first two train cars off the tracks.

At the time of the crash, 95 passengers were onboard the train, and at least four people have been transported to nearby hospitals with injuries. First responders remain on scene tonight as authorities investigate the grade-crossing collision.

Hoping everyone onboard makes a full recovery. Have you ever seen an 18-wheeler get stuck or cross late at a railroad crossing? Share your thoughts below 👇

#Amtrak #TrainDerailment

“WE KNEW EXACTLY WHO KILLED OUR MEN IN BENGHAZI. WE HAD THEIR LOCATIONS. AND WASHINGTON TOLD US TO STAND DOWN.”

On September 11, 2012, four Americans lost their lives during the coordinated terrorist assault on the U.S. diplomatic compound and CIA annex in Benghazi, Libya: Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens, Sean Smith, and former Navy SEALs Tyrone "Rone" Woods and Glen "Bub" Doherty.

While Washington officials publicly claimed the tragedy was a "spontaneous protest over a video," former senior CIA targeting officer Sarah Adams (code-named "Superbad") sat down on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #116) to expose the reality of what intelligence operatives found on the ground.

In her own words:

“For years, the public was told that Benghazi was a spontaneous protest over an internet video. It was an outright lie.”

“Our targeting teams tracked down every single terrorist involved in that attack. We identified the exact network, the leadership, the safe houses, and the specific individuals who fired the mortars that killed Tyrone Woods and Glen Doherty on that rooftop.”

“We had actionable, real-time intelligence packets on them. We knew the streets they walked on, the houses they slept in, and their phone numbers.”

“We handed the packages up the chain, ready to strike, and leadership repeatedly refused to authorize the missions. They sat on their hands because killing those terrorists would have forced politicians to admit that their original narrative was completely fabricated.”

“Leaving the killers of American heroes free to walk the streets was the greatest betrayal I witnessed in my entire career.”

Key revelations from Sarah Adams’ investigation in Benghazi: Know Thy Enemy:

The attack was meticulously planned by Ansar al-Sharia and allied Al-Qaeda cells, not a disorganized riot.

 CIA targeting officers assembled complete, actionable kinetic strike packages identifying the exact mortar operators who targeted the annex rooftop.

High-level leadership repeatedly refused to greenlight direct-action missions to capture or eliminate the perpetrators to avoid undermining official administration narratives.

The Cost of Betrayal: Dozens of terrorists directly implicated in the deaths of American personnel remained free across North Africa for years.

Denmark just voted 109-0 to allow more U.S. military in Greenland.

On November 19, Danish lawmakers unanimously ratified a new security agreement with the United States covering Greenland.

The vote was 109-0.
No opposition. No abstentions.

The deal clears the way for expanded U.S. military presence, including potential new bases and missile defense systems on the island.

It comes after years of back-and-forth — including public comments from President Trump about the strategic value of Greenland that many people dismissed or mocked at the time.

Now Denmark itself has given formal, unanimous approval for a deeper American military footprint in the Arctic.

Some will see this as proof that the original focus on Greenland’s importance was right all along.
Others will frame it as a pragmatic response to growing Arctic competition, separate from any earlier rhetoric.

Either way, the vote is real, and the door is now open for more U.S. forces in one of the most strategically important places on the planet.

Was Trump right on Greenland?

“THE FIRST RULE OF SURVIVING AN AMBUSH: FIGHT THROUGH THE INITIAL SHOCK.” — When three MS-13 gang members opened fire point-blank into her patrol car window at 3:30 AM, Officer Ann Carrizales didn't collapse or curl into a defensive posture. Her Marine Corps muscle memory took over: bleeding from the cheek and chest, she returned fire through her windshield and initiated a 20-mile pursuit at 100 mph.

“When that round hit my face, it felt like being struck with a baseball bat. But in the Marine Corps, you're conditioned to push past the shock and stay in the fight. Giving up was never an option. My only thought was: You picked the wrong cop, and you're not getting away with this.”

 Officer Ann Carrizales, Former USMC Military Police & Stafford Police Department

 Ambush statistics show that most fatal encounters occur within the first three seconds when victims freeze or attempt to retreat without returning fire. Carrizales absorbed rounds to both her face and Kevlar chest vest, immediately clearing leather and returning lethal fire into the threat vehicle to disrupt the shooters' momentum.

Recognizing that transitioning out of the patrol unit in the kill zone would leave her exposed, she engaged the suspects directly through her cruiser glass, suppressing the vehicle before they could deliver follow-up headshots.

 Despite significant blood loss and acoustic trauma from enclosed gunfire, she broadcasted suspect descriptions, vehicle coordinates, and direction of travel across regional dispatch channels, driving over 100 mph from Stafford into Houston until the suspects crashed out and were taken into custody.

 Prior to joining the Stafford Police Department, Carrizales served as a Military Police officer and competed as a champion boxer in the Marine Corps, building the neurological resilience and stress-inoculation required to execute dynamic tactical decisions while severely wounded.

“14 DIRECT HITS WITH .45 ACP. SIX MORTAL ORGAN WOUNDS. AND HE WAS STILL FIRING.” — The harrowing 2008 Illinois shootout that permanently changed modern police loadouts, proving why handguns are marginal stoppers and why Officer Tim Gramins never goes on patrol with fewer than 145 rounds.

“People ask me all the time, ‘Why do you carry so much ammunition? Are you paranoid?’ I tell them: It’s not paranoia. It’s preparation. I’ve been down to my last four bullets in a gunfight with a man who absorbed six fatal hits and kept trying to kill me. I will never let that happen again.”

 Officer Tim Gramins, Skokie Police Department Firearms Instructor

Tactical Breakdown: The 56-Second Gunfight
The Immediate Ambush: On a quiet August afternoon in Skokie, Illinois, Officer Tim Gramins initiated a traffic stop on a bank robbery suspect. Before Gramins could unbuckle his seatbelt, the suspect stepped out and immediately opened fire at close range, dumping rounds through Gramins' cruiser windshield.

 Gramins fired 33 rounds of heavy .45 ACP from his Glock 21, scoring 14 direct torso hits. Despite suffering six non-survivable wounds—including damage to his heart, both lungs, liver, diaphragm, and kidney—the suspect continued maneuvering, reloading, and firing for nearly a minute on sheer adrenaline and rage.

Burning through his primary magazine and two belt reloads, Gramins found himself pinned down behind the suspect's vehicle with only four rounds remaining in his entire arsenal. Recognizing that center-mass hits were not stopping the threat, he took deliberate aim under incoming fire and delivered three headshots to finally neutralize the gunman.

 Prior to the incident, Gramins carried a standard patrol loadout of 47 rounds. Realizing that a second suspect would have left him with an empty gun, Gramins transitioned his carry setup to 145 rounds of 9mm—carrying three 17-round spare magazines on his duty belt, two 33-round extended magazines in his active-shooter plate carrier, and a backup firearm.

 Handgun calibers (.45 ACP, .40 S&W, 9mm) do not create catastrophic hydrostatic shock like rifle rounds. Unless a round disrupts the brainstem or upper cervical spine, a determined adversary can remain functional for 30 to 60 seconds even with zero blood pressure.

 High-speed, dynamic gunfights burn through ammunition at roughly 3 to 4 rounds per second. When movement, vehicle cover, and adrenaline degrade precision, capacity is often the difference between winning and running dry.

When multiple center-mass hits fail to alter an attacker's behavior within seconds, officers must immediately recognize the failure to stop and transition to cranial or pelvic vault targets.

Officer Gramins' survival sparked a nationwide debate on patrol carry capacity versus everyday comfort. How many spare magazines should patrol officers and concealed carriers reasonably carry? Share your thoughts below.

The B-21 stealth bomber just dropped its first weapon.

In early November, a B-21 Raider flying out of Edwards Air Force Base successfully released a conventional weapon for the first time.

This is a major milestone.
The test moves the aircraft from pure flight testing into a functional weapons platform.

The B-21 is designed to be the next-generation penetrating bomber — harder to detect, able to operate in heavily defended airspace, and built to carry both conventional and nuclear weapons.

The first operational bombers are still scheduled to arrive in 2027.

For now, this successful weapons release shows the program is advancing on schedule and proving it can actually put steel on target.

Some will look at this and see a clear signal aimed at peer competitors.
Others will say it’s simply the next logical step in a long testing program.

Either way, the Raider is no longer just flying.
It’s now dropping weapons.

Should China be worried?

Nothing builds unbreakable bonds quite like humping a heavy crew-served weapon through the dense, unforgiving timberlines of Hohenfels!

Soldiers with the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Armored Division navigate complex field scenarios during Exercise Combined Resolve 27-01 at the Joint Multinational Readiness Center (JMRC) in Hohenfels, Germany. 

Hauling heavy weapon systems and tripods on foot across rugged, wooded terrain demands elite physical endurance, seamless communication, and relentless small-unit teamwork. 

1ABCT and 1AD units are putting their tactical proficiency to the test in Europe, executing realistic multi-domain field exercises designed to sharpen combat readiness alongside NATO allies. 

Whether pushing through simulated enemy contact or managing heavy loads in austere environments, infantry teamwork remains the definitive bedrock of mission success.

Cpl. Baughman was deployed with the 187th Infantry Regiment in September 2005 for a year-long deployment to Iraq. On July 17, 2006, Baughman's Humvee was part of a convoy participating in patrol operations in the city of Bayji, Iraq. His Humvee was hit by an RPG, severely injuring him. Later that day, Baughman died from his injuries.

On July 19, 2006, Baughman was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal and the Purple Heart for going beyond the call of duty and giving his life for his fellow soldiers.

A grenade landed on the rooftop.
He covered it with his body.
He was only 21. 

November 21, 2010.
Marjah, Afghanistan.

Cpl. Kyle Carpenter and Lance Cpl. Nick Eufrazio were on a rooftop when an enemy grenade landed between them.

Without hesitation, Carpenter threw himself on top of it.

The blast nearly killed him.
He lost an eye, suffered massive injuries to his face and body, and spent years recovering through dozens of surgeries.

But his friend survived.

Sixteen years later, the story still hits the same way.
A 21-year-old Marine made a split-second decision that most people will never face — and chose someone else’s life over his own.

He lived.
He recovered.
He received the Medal of Honor.

Some acts of courage are so pure they don’t need much explanation.

This was one of them.

Asked if Putin is a friend to America, Trump said this:
“I can’t speak to America.” 

At a White House news conference on November 20, President Trump was pressed on his relationship with Vladimir Putin.

He has repeatedly called Putin his “friend.”
When a reporter asked whether Putin is also a friend to the United States, Trump answered:
“I can’t speak to America.”

He went on to defend the personal relationship, saying he has a “fantastic” one with the Russian leader and that such relationships keep the country safer.

The exchange quickly stood out.
One moment Trump is describing a personal friendship.
The next he’s declining to say whether that friendship extends to the country he leads.

Supporters hear a president prioritizing personal diplomacy and results.
Critics hear a line that draws a strange separation between the president and the nation.

Either way, the quote is now out there.

What do you make of that answer?

The U.S. government just released decades of archived "Bigfoot Files" — and the 1982 Forest Service report is raising eyebrows.

Buried in newly unsealed USDA records is a June 1982 investigation by Wildlife Biologist Rodney L. Johnson into 15-inch tracks found in Washington's Mill Creek Watershed inside the Umatilla National Forest.

After inspecting two sites, Johnson listed eight reasons he believed the prints were "made by something other than a 300 pound plus two footed being" — noting an unchanging four-foot stride regardless of slope, shallower imprints than his own boots, brushed-aside pine needles, and zero heel or toe slippage on steep mud.

Yet on the very next page, he admitted something remarkable — "If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail. The 'print' marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate. They appear very natural."

Elaborate 1982 hoax or something unexplained in the Pacific Northwest? Drop your take below.

#BigfootFiles #USForestService

“SEVEN BULLETS. A SHATTERED JAW. AND THE INDOMITABLE WILL TO WIN.” — In January 2008, Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office detective and SWAT operator Jared Reston chased a shoplifter outside a shopping mall. Seconds later, he took a point-blank .45 caliber round straight through his chin that shattered his lower jaw, followed by six more hits to his chest and limbs. Lying on his back in the dirt, Reston kept his vision focused, unholstered his Glock 22, and fought his way back to his feet to end the threat.

“That’s how law enforcement works: you can go from a foot chase to full-on fighting for your life in half a second. When you get shot in the face, you have two choices: lie there and die, or stay in the fight and win. My thought was simple: He’s not going home today, I am.”

— Detective Jared Reston, Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office & Medal of Valor Recipient

Tactical Breakdown: Surviving 7 Point-Blank Rounds
The Lethal Transition: Chasing an armed shoplifting suspect across a parking lot outside Regency Square Mall in Jacksonville, Florida, Reston closed the distance when the suspect spun with a stolen .45 ACP handgun, firing 12 rounds at point-blank range.

Absorbing Massive Trauma: Seven rounds struck Reston: one entered his chin and fractured his mandible into pieces, three rounds hit his concealed Kevlar vest directly over vital organs, and three more tore through his elbow, hip, and thigh.

Returning Fire from the Ground: Knocked violently onto his back in the mud and choking on blood, Reston refused to enter psychological shock. He cleared his holster, acquired his front sight, and fired 14 rounds from his Glock 22 (.40 S&W), hitting the advancing gunman repeatedly.

Closing the Distance & CNS Stop: Despite absorbing multiple torso hits, the suspect continued firing. Reston fought his way back onto his feet, closed to contact distance, and delivered immediate central nervous system headshots to terminate the threat.

Weapon-Mounted Light Standoff Advantage: During the grapple, the bezel of Reston's Streamlight weapon-mounted light extended past the muzzle, creating the mechanical standoff necessary to keep his pistol in battery and fire contact shots without jamming the slide.

The Road to the Medal of Valor: Following multiple reconstructive surgeries on his face and jaw, Reston returned to active SWAT service, was awarded the Florida Law Enforcement Officer of the Year, and received the Presidential Public Safety Officer Medal of Valor in Washington, D.C.

On Christmas Eve 2007, Royal Marines Commando Mark Ormrod was on a routine foot patrol in Helmand Province, Afghanistan, when he triggered a concealed improvised explosive device while moving to provide covering fire for his teammates.

Evacuated by helicopter to Camp Bastion and then flown to Birmingham, Ormrod lost both legs above the knee and his right arm above the elbow, becoming Britain's first triple amputee to survive the Afghanistan conflict. After waking up in the hospital, he proposed to his girlfriend, Becky, and she said yes.

Told he might never walk again, Ormrod spent years in rehabilitation learning to use prosthetics, left the Royal Marines in 2010, and went on to win multiple medals at the Invictus Games while advocating for wounded veterans.

#MarkOrmrod #RoyalMarines

A sobering crisis inside America's top intelligence and cyber commands is drawing urgent scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

At least 11 National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command workers — including military personnel and civilians, largely based at Fort Meade, Maryland — have died by suicide over roughly the past year.

Lawmakers are demanding answers and pushing for $11 million in mental health and resilience funding requested by NSA and Cyber Command leader Gen. Joshua Rudd, along with placing security-cleared counselors directly inside classified workspaces. While officials say each case involved complex personal factors, former insiders warn of relentless burnout from high-tempo "deployed-in-place" cyber operations.

Doris Miller, known as “Dorie” to shipmates and friends, was a U.S. Navy Sailor recognized for his bravery during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. He was the first African American recipient of the Navy Cross.

Developing out of the Persian Gulf — air raid sirens are sounding and loud explosions are being heard in Bahrain amid initial reports that Iran has launched drones toward U.S. bases.

Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, has already intercepted three waves of Iranian drone attacks in recent days targeting U.S. radar and military installations at Al-Riffa and Sheikh Isa air bases, prompting U.S. retaliatory precision strikes on an IRGC missile site on Qeshm Island earlier this week.

We are monitoring CENTCOM and Bahraini officials for confirmation on interceptions, damage, or casualties as the situation develops.

Follow for live updates as more details come in.

#Bahrain #Iran #USMilitary

NIGHT COLLISION OFF CORONADO. INJURED IN THE CRASH, HE DIVED INTO TOTAL DARKNESS TO PULL HIS BROTHER OUT.

Operating at speed in the open ocean at midnight leaves zero room for error.

Returning from nighttime tactical training off Southern California with Naval Special Warfare Logistics Support Unit 1, a special operations support boat struck a submerged rock jetty in the dark. The violent impact ejected crew members into the freezing surf, leaving one sailor knocked unconscious and floating facedown in pitch-black waters.

Injured and concussed from the initial collision himself, Utilitiesman 1st Class Steven Schumacher saw his teammate in the black chop. Disregarding his own trauma, Schumacher dove straight over the gunwale into the Pacific, fought the swell to reach his unresponsive teammate, and hauled his brother back aboard to clear his airway until emergency medical teams arrived.

According to the official ceremony announcement from Navy.mil, Schumacher received the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for heroism under life-threatening conditions.

Diving into freezing black ocean water while bleeding and injured to save a teammate defines brotherhood in the special warfare community.

Col. Lewis Millett
Lewis Millett joined the Army in 1941 but got tired of waiting for the U.S. to invade someone, so he deserted to Canada and got himself deployed to London. When American entered the war, he jumped back under the Stars and Bars and twice saved men in his unit from certain death before his desertion charges caught up with him.

Lewis Millett joined the Army in 1941 but got tired of waiting for the U.S. to invade someone, so he deserted to Canada and got himself deployed to London. When America entered the war, he jumped back under the Stars and Bars and twice saved men in his unit from certain death before his desertion charges caught up with him.

He led an assault under fire in Panama in 1989.
37 years later, he finally got the medal. 
In December 1989, during Operation Just Cause, then-First Lieutenant Robert Gaddis was in the middle of the fight in Panama.

He led ambushes against enemy vehicles under heavy fire.
He moved alone through defensive positions.
He took command of a stalled assault and personally led the attack that cleared the objective.

Two days later, when Panamanian forces counterattacked with automatic weapons, mortars, and grenades, he helped move wounded soldiers and civilians to safety while continuing to direct his troops.

On November 19, 2026 — nearly 37 years later — retired Col. Robert Gaddis finally received the Bronze Star Medal with “V” device for valor.

Some awards arrive quickly.
This one took a lifetime.

Better late than never… but why did it take so long?

President Trump says he plans to make a "permanent" deal with Iran — one that no future U.S. president can undo.

Speaking with Fox News on Saturday, Trump said any agreement must permanently block Tehran from ever acquiring a nuclear weapon, downplaying regime change while noting the U.S. is now dealing with a third group of Iranian leadership.

Meanwhile, Qatari mediators met with officials in Tehran today as Iran demands an end to the U.S. naval blockade and refuses to ship its 60%-enriched uranium abroad — and Israeli officials warn Iran is rapidly rebuilding its missile production underground.

In 2004, US Marine 1stSgt. Brad Kasal was engaged in a firefight with insurgents during the Second Battle of Fallujah. He was hit by seven 7.62mm rounds and 47 pieces of shrapnel from a fragmentation grenade. While fighting, he used his body to shield another Marine. He was responsible for saving the lives of several Marines under his command. After being taken out of the house by his Marines, he was still holding his M9 Beretta pistol and his Ka-Bar knife. He refused to lie on a litter to deny the enemy the satisfaction of seeing him in a supine position. After arriving at the field hospital, it was determined that he had lost 60% of his blood. It was later determined that he had over 100 puncture wounds. As a result of his injuries, he lost four inches of bone in his right leg. He has undergone 21 surgeries to repair the injuries to his leg. For his actions, he was awarded several medals, including the Navy Cross for valor. He retired in 2018 from the Marine Corps at the rank of Sgt. Major.

“THE BRAVEST THING I HAVE EVER SEEN IN 17 YEARS HAPPENED ON THAT NIGHT.” — DEVGRU / SEAL Team 6 Operator DJ Shipley on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the rawest combat breakdowns in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show, former DEVGRU assault team operator DJ Shipley recounted the night in Iraq when heavy machine-gun fire caught his team in open ground, leaving teammates gravely wounded in the dark.

In his own words:

“I remember looking over and seeing Jay [Jason Redman]. I remember him sitting upright, and I watched him get shot one more time, right in the face. He hit the ground so hard you knew he was dead.

We’re stuck behind a tractor tire that’s halfway out of the ground, serving no purpose, taking fire from every angle. It’s pitch black.

The bravest thing I have ever seen in 17 years happened on that night.

I watched Maddie get up and run forward after he had already been shot. He grabs our corpsman and starts dragging him backwards. Just like in the movies, the corpsman pulls his pistol, shooting into the woodline.

Maddie gets shot again—it spins him around and dumps him. He gets back up, grabs him, and gets shot again. Dumps him, gets back up, and continues dragging him until we got them all behind that tire.

Jason took one to the face that basically removed his jaw, removed his nose, and you could look inside him. Maddie’s arm was completely shattered. We basically just dog-piled on top of them. Plates on plates, just trying to build up a human wall so our brothers wouldn't take another bullet.”

Against all medical odds, Jason Redman survived the devastating facial gunshot wound, enduring dozens of reconstructive surgeries and going on to inspire millions across the veteran community.

Getting shot, knocked to the dirt, getting back up under machine-gun fire, and continuing to drag your wounded brothers to cover is the purest embodiment of brotherhood under fire.

Marriner Richards was a 19-year-old United States Marine from Syracuse, Utah, remembered by his family as a natural leader who was always willing to lend an ear to those in need. Stationed at the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms, California, his promising young life took a sudden turn on the night of Friday, November 6, 2026. After visiting the nearby Tortoise Rock Casino on the edge of the Mojave Desert, he walked away on foot without a vehicle, vanishing into the night. When he failed to return to his post, military police reported him missing the following day, launching a desperate two-week search across the vast and unforgiving desert terrain bordering Joshua Tree National Park.

Determined to bring their son home, Marriner's parents, Brock and Brooke Richards, traveled from Utah to California to join the search on the ground. They were met with an outpouring of love and support as dozens of local residents, fellow Marines, law enforcement deputies with off-road vehicles and helicopters, and even neighbors and church members who drove down from Utah banded together to comb the desert. For two agonizing weeks, volunteers searched tirelessly in the hopes of finding him safe. That hope came to a heartbreaking end on Friday, November 20, when a member of the search party discovered Marriner's body inside an abandoned building just a few miles from both the casino and his base. The San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department later confirmed the tragic news that the young Marine had died by suicide, leaving his family, his community in Utah, and his fellow service members mourning a life lost far too soon.
